messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventy‑two miles from the nearest city, Karim works the same strip of wheat that his grandfather tended, the sun hot on his back and the soil cool in his hands. A quiet, middle‑aged man in a faded blue shirt, he married Fatima ten years ago and the house he shares with her is filled with the scent of cumin and the chatter of their two children. The day his life shifted began with a familiar rhythm: he was hauling a sack of seed when a stranger in a dark jacket appeared beside the ridge. The stranger’s eyes flicked at Karim, his voice low, “You’ve been working all day, why not let the others help?” Karim laughed nervously, but the man pressed a knife into his side, the blade’s cold hiss echoing in his ears. Karim’s breath hitched; his heart began to pound, the same racing he now feels whenever he hears footsteps too close. The stranger vanished as quickly as he had appeared, leaving a bruise on Karim’s left thigh and a lingering sense of danger that has followed him for the past years. The triggers that haunt Karim are simple and intimate. Whenever his own heart starts to race or his skin sweats, he feels the same terror that the stranger’s knife had inflicted. The odor of sweat, the subtle musk of bodies in close proximity, and the sight of someone acting suspiciously—especially when they seem to eye him with the same intent—send shivers down his spine. He recalls, in flashes, the way the man’s breath was hot against his neck, the metallic taste of blood on his tongue. Those sensations have become a barometer of threat; a pounding heart or the scent of sweat immediately brings him back to that day, even if the event is not in view. These triggers have steered Karim toward specific ways of coping. When his heart thumps in the quiet of the evening, he retreats into the barn, throwing himself into tasks—reaching for a missing seed bag, tightening a loose nail—so the mind has no room for the memory that the knife had threatened to seize it. The more he avoids those moments, the more he believes that staying busy is the only shield against the unknown threat. The fear of a heartbeat out of rhythm or a stray scent has convinced him that if he simply works until his hands are calloused, the danger will be forgotten. When a distant echo of someone walking near his fence startles him, he locks the gate, turns his back on the road, and refuses to let anyone pass. In this way, the triggers have forged an avoidance pattern, a self‑protective strategy that he has woven into every day of his life. The memory of that assault is a puzzle of fragments. Karim tells himself that the event feels like it belongs to someone else; he cannot describe the scene with a continuous thread. He speaks of a knife, a stranger’s face, the sting of metal, but when he tries to explain the sequence, the words slip away. The recollection feels disjointed, as though he is peering through a broken window, seeing bits of a story but missing the edges. He has long said that the memory is too fragmented to make sense of, as if the pieces were cut out by a force that refuses to allow a coherent picture. This alien, incomplete memory has left Karim feeling detached from the event, as if it were not truly his own. Because the memory is so disordered, Karim has found that the more he ruminates about it, the more he is driven to seek vengeance. He has begun to imagine ways to make the assailant feel the same panic he felt when the knife was thrust in his side. He tells himself that he will wait until the man is next seen on the ridge, that he will confront him. These thoughts become a mental rehearsal of retribution, an attempt to regain a sense of agency that the fragmented memory has stolen. The fragmented, alien memory feeds the need to restore control, and the rumination, in turn, sharpens his resolve to find the perpetrator. In this cycle, the memory’s disjointedness and the urge for revenge reinforce each other, keeping Karim locked in a loop of obsessive thinking that never settles. Karim’s avoidance has spilled into his daily routine. He has stopped attending the monthly community meeting on crop rotation, choosing instead to stay on the farm from dawn to dusk. The extra work has filled the silence that his heart racing would otherwise bring, but it has also caused tension at home. Fatima notices that Karim seems distant, that he rarely smiles, and that his eyes are always looking out over the fields as if expecting someone to appear. Karim’s relentless labor, while providing a distraction, also keeps him from confronting the pain; the farm becomes a refuge and a prison. The moment that finally brought Karim to the clinic was a storm on the ridge that shook the old oak tree near his barn. A sudden, sudden tremor sent a shiver through the soil, and Karim’s heart began to pound. He closed his eyes, feeling the familiar rush of panic, and realized that he could no longer stay hidden in his work. Fatima had spoken to him before, urging him to seek help, but he had resisted. Now, when the storm’s wind slammed against the windows and his heart thumped like a drum, he understood that the cycle had tightened so far that it threatened his own safety and his relationship. He is now afraid that his relentless avoidance and rumination might drive a wedge between him and Fatima, but he also hopes that confronting the memory and its triggers might free him from the relentless loop that has kept him working the same field for years, heart racing, mind wandering to revenge, body sweating, and memory fragments scattered across his mind.
